before: A spike count $N_i$ increases outgoing activation $s_i$ by one; between spikes it decays over time $\tau$. The fixed weight $W_{ij}$ sends cell $j$'s activation to receiver $i$; bias $b_i$ completes total input $g_i$. [Chapter 1; paper Eqs. 7–9](../chapters/ch-foundations.html#sec-memory-spikes).
after: Each spike increases outgoing activation $s_i$ by one; the count process $N_i$ records these events. Between spikes, activation decays over time $\tau$. The fixed weight $W_{ij}$ sends cell $j$'s activation to receiver $i$; bias $b_i$ completes total input $g_i$. [Chapter 1; paper Eqs. 7–9](../chapters/ch-foundations.html#sec-memory-spikes).

before: Kac–Rice multiplies height density at $q$ by mean positive spatial slope there. Stationary Gaussian height and slope are independent. Add $Q(q)=\Pr(Z>q)$, $Z\sim N(0,1)$, for a field already active at the left end of a track of length $L$. [Chapter 10; S9–S13 and main Eq. 8](../chapters/ch-place-fields.html#sec-place-kac-rice).
after: Kac–Rice multiplies height density at $q$ by mean positive part of the spatial slope there. Stationary Gaussian height and slope are independent. Add $Q(q)=\Pr(Z>q)$, $Z\sim N(0,1)$, for a field already active at the left end of a track of length $L$. [Chapter 10; S9–S13 and main Eq. 8](../chapters/ch-place-fields.html#sec-place-kac-rice).

before: Divide active and inactive spatial fractions by the same upcrossing density to obtain mean field length $\mu_s$ and gap length $\mu_g$. Their ratio gives active fraction; invert the Gaussian upper tail and crossing scale. [Chapter 10; Methods S3](../chapters/ch-place-fields.html#sec-place-inference).
after: Divide active and inactive spatial fractions by the same upcrossing density to obtain mean field length $\mu_s$ and gap length $\mu_g$. The ratio $\mu_s/(\mu_s+\mu_g)$ gives active fraction; invert the Gaussian upper tail and crossing scale. [Chapter 10; Methods S3](../chapters/ch-place-fields.html#sec-place-inference).
